questions.stem: Group means are: treat pre 10, treat post 13, control pre 9, control post 11. What is the difference in differences?
questions.explanation: The treated change is 3 and the control change is 2, so the difference in differences is 1.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: What a fractional factorial assumes
questions.stem: Explain the tradeoff made by a fractional factorial design.

answer.exemplar: It trades the ability to estimate some high-order interactions for a smaller number of experimental runs.

questions.explanation: The design sacrifices certain interaction estimates to reduce experimental effort.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: Why intention-to-treat keeps every assigned patient
questions.stem: A trial assigns 60 patients to treatment and 60 to control, but 10 treated patients are lost. Under intention-to-treat, what is the treatment group size?

options.text: The treatment group size is 120.
The treatment group size is 50.
The treatment group size is 70.
The treatment group size is 60.

questions.explanation: Intention-to-treat retains all 60 assigned patients in the treatment group.

questions.topic: Error degrees of freedom in a completely randomised design
questions.stem: A completely randomised design has 24 observations across 4 treatment groups. What are the error degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation: Twenty-four minus 4 gives 20 error degrees of freedom.

questions.subject: STATISTICS
questions.topic: Error degrees of freedom in a randomised block design
questions.stem: Explain why a randomised block design can have fewer error degrees of freedom than a completely randomised design with the same n.

answer.exemplar: Blocking consumes degrees of freedom for block effects, leaving fewer for error, but it reduces nuisance variation.

questions.explanation: The tradeoff is fewer error degrees of freedom in exchange for reduced nuisance variation.
questions.hint: Blocks consume df but reduce noise.
